What do export controls between Washington and Beijing have in common with the Houthis’ ability to disrupt shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb? Both represent the embrace of chokepoints as an economic weapon. So, what tools are in this new arsenal? How are they enforced? And how will they change the global economy?
Edward Fishman deployed these very tools during his time serving in the U.S. Defense, State, and Treasury Departments. In Chokepoints: American Power in the Age of Economic Warfare, he argues that the United States built a playbook that is now being used against it, whether offensively or in self-defense. Fishman joins FP Live to unpack what this new economic warfare costs the global economy and U.S. power.

Host and Guests

Edward Fishman

Author, Chokepoints: American Power in the Age of Economic Warfare

Edward Fishman teaches at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs and is a senior research scholar at the Center on Global Energy Policy. He is also a senior fellow and director of the Maurice R. Greenberg Center for Geoeconomics at the Council on Foreign Relations. During the Obama administration, he was a top sanctions official at the U.S. State Department. He is the author of the bestselling book, Chokepoints: American Power in the Age of Economic Warfare.

Energy After the Shock

July 29, 2026

Oil prices are once again on the rise—and this time, they may not come down so quickly. With the Strait of Hormuz once again shut down and the Houthis attempting to block Saudi exports through the Red Sea, crude prices seem set to soar. In addition, global reservoirs of crude haven’t been restored, and China may drop its export curbs. Beyond the immediate price shock, how will countries and companies adapt their behavior in the longer term? Daniel Yergin, energy guru and economic historian who recently wrote The New Map, joined FP Live to share his insights.

Where the Iran Conflict Goes From Here

July 20, 2026

As the United States and Iran hit the escalate button once again, what will it take for both sides to pull back? One advisor the White House could have turned to was Nate Swanson, a career State Department official who served most recently as an Iran negotiator. Outside of government, he accurately predicted how Iran would respond to U.S. strikes and how it might overplay its hand after signing the memorandum of understanding. Where does Swanson see the conflict headed next?

Is Trans-Atlanticism Dead? A Debate.

July 14, 2026

U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term has forced a reckoning: Can the trans-Atlantic relationship be salvaged, or is the damage permanent? Nathalie Tocci argues it cannot be rebuilt as it was: the liberal order that gave trans-Atlanticism its context is gone, and a fundamental breach of trust has occurred. Alexandra de Hoop Scheffer sees it differently: Trans-Atlanticism was never only based on values and Europe’s surge in defense spending signals its emergence as a geopolitically mature partner. They joined FP’s Ravi Agrawal for a debate.

Ukraine’s New Momentum?

July 9, 2026

When NATO leaders convened this week in Ankara, Turkey, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky again pressed them to cement their support for Kyiv. But this time, he could argue that Ukraine’s long-range drones have brought the war home to Russians, a strain that even President Vladimir Putin has recently acknowledged. Can battlefield momentum translate into movement in the peace talks? How much does Kyiv still need Washington? Dmytro Kuleba, Ukraine’s foreign minister from 2020 to 2024, joined FP’s Ravi Agrawal to assess where the war goes from here.
